sentences.text: Cities that charge drivers to enter their centres get less traffic and better air.
London's congestion charge, launched in 2003, cut traffic entering the zone by roughly 15 per cent and initial congestion by about 30 per cent, according to Transport for London.
Stockholm's 2006 trial, made permanent in 2007, reduced vehicles crossing the cordon by around 20 per cent and helped cut emissions.
Singapore has priced road entry since 1975.
Revenue funds buses, trains, and walking and cycling.
Drivers pay for the space and pollution they impose on everyone else.
The evidence is clear: charging works.
A fee can reduce traffic, but that does not prove it is fair or the best way to improve a city.
In Greater Manchester’s 2008 referendum, 79.1% voted against a proposed congestion-charge scheme.
That is a warning against imposing charges without public consent and dependable alternatives to driving.

London’s early traffic reductions also did not guarantee lasting congestion relief: Transport for London reported that congestion had risen again by 2006–07, citing factors including roadworks and reduced road capacity.
Charges can burden workers and small businesses that cannot readily switch to public transport.
Cities should improve alternatives and target specific bottlenecks before making access depend on ability to pay.
Stockholm answers Manchester: after a seven-month trial, 51.3% voted yes in 2006, and the charge became permanent in 2007.
Consent follows visible results, not imposition.
London's later congestion rise came with roadworks and reallocated road capacity; TfL still recorded roughly 15% less traffic entering the zone.
Free entry is not neutral: it subsidises drivers who pollute and occupy scarce space.
Revenue funds buses, which serve workers and small-business customers.
Burden falls hardest when cities have no alternative.
Pair charging with bus lanes, discounts, and a trial-then-referendum path, and the fairness objection collapses.
Stockholm shows that a trial and referendum can win support there; it does not answer Manchester’s 79.1% rejection or establish consent elsewhere.
Nor does spending revenue on buses make the charge fair to workers who must drive and cannot use those buses.
A flat entry fee also treats a low-emission car like a more polluting one, even though their emissions differ.
If the aim is cleaner air, London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone targets vehicle emissions directly.
Cities should improve transport and tackle pollution without making access to their centres depend on ability to pay.
You accept London's ULEZ, which is itself a charge to enter the centre.
So the dispute is design, not principle.
Make the fee emissions- and time-varied, as Singapore's Electronic Road Pricing does, with discounts for residents and exemptions for disabled drivers.
Manchester rejected one under-specified package; Stockholm's trial-then-vote won 51.3 per cent.
Free entry is not fair to those who breathe traffic or wait on clogged buses.
It rations space by queue and delay, charging workers time instead of money.
Revenue can fund the alternatives that make charging acceptable.
ULEZ does not prove that cities should charge everyone for entering their centres: it applies to vehicles that fail emissions standards, rather than imposing a general access fee.
Singapore’s time- and location-varying road pricing shows that design can be more targeted, but it does not remove the burden on drivers with no practical alternative.
Discounts and exemptions also complicate administration and leave some people paying for journeys they cannot avoid.
And calling congestion a “time charge” does not make a cash fee fair; both costs matter.
Cities should first improve public transport and reduce pollution at source, then consider narrowly targeted charges where evidence and public consent support them.
Congestion pricing works, and the evidence spans five decades.
Singapore pioneered it in 1975 with its Area Licensing Scheme and has kept road pricing ever since.
London introduced its congestion charge in February 2003, and Transport for London reported that traffic entering the zone fell by about 18 percent in the first year.
Stockholm ran a trial in 2006, made the charge permanent in 2007, and saw traffic across the cordon drop by roughly 20 percent.
New York began charging most cars nine dollars at peak times in January 2025.
The principle is simple.
Road space in a dense centre is scarce, and pricing it lets buses, deliveries and emergency vehicles move while raising money for transit.
Fewer cars do not guarantee lasting relief.
Transport for London’s 2008 monitoring report found congestion in the original charging zone had returned to pre-charge levels, despite traffic remaining below its earlier level.
Reduced road capacity, including roadworks, helped explain that result.
Pricing cannot substitute for managing streets properly.
Nor does willingness to pay measure the importance of a journey: a wealthy commuter can absorb a charge more easily than a low-paid worker with poor transit options.
Cities should improve public transport and target parking and bottlenecks before imposing an entry fee that allocates access partly by income.
My opponent's own evidence makes my case.
TfL found traffic stayed below pre-charge levels even as congestion returned, because road space was deliberately reallocated to bus lanes, pedestrians and a surge of utility works.
TfL concluded that without the charge, congestion would have been worse.
The charge freed capacity; the city chose to spend it on other users.
On fairness, in dense centres most low-paid workers already commute by bus or train, not car, so an entry fee mainly charges wealthier drivers.
London's net charge revenue must by law go to transport, and New York's toll funds the MTA's capital programme.
Stockholm voters approved their charge in a 2006 referendum after experiencing it.
Your argument shifts from relieving congestion to reallocating road space.
Those are different goals: London’s experience shows an entry fee does not guarantee faster journeys.
And even if most low-paid workers use transit, that does not protect those whose shifts or destinations make driving necessary.
Average income is not a fairness test for individual journeys.
London itself recognises unequal impacts: eligible residents within the charging zone receive a 90 percent discount.
That concession also shows that charging every journey is not indispensable.
Earmarking revenue for transport is welcome, but it does not establish that an entry charge is fairer than alternative funding.
Reallocating road space is not a change of goal.
It is how relieving congestion pays off: a bus lane moves far more people than a car lane, so fewer cars and more buses is faster travel for most travellers.
Stockholm shows the direct effect too.
Queuing times on its inner approaches fell sharply after charging began.
On individual hardship, my opponent proves my point.
Charges can be targeted.
London exempts Blue Badge holders and discounts residents, so the necessary journeys my opponent worries about can be protected without abandoning pricing.
The alternatives fall short.
Parking rules ignore through-traffic and free roads stay gridlocked.
Pricing is the only proven tool that manages demand and funds transit together.
Your “only proven tool” claim overlooks Nottingham’s Workplace Parking Levy, introduced in 2012.
It charges employers providing more than ten liable workplace parking spaces, and its revenue helped fund the city’s tram expansion.
Cities can discourage car commuting and fund transit without charging everyone crossing a boundary.

Nor do London’s concessions protect every necessary journey: Blue Badge eligibility is not a test of whether someone’s shift or destination requires driving, and a resident discount does nothing for an essential worker living outside the zone.
Stockholm demonstrates that charges can reduce queues; it does not establish that entry fees are the fairest policy for every city.
Cities should adopt carefully designed rent control because sudden rent spikes can displace residents faster than new housing can be built.

Evidence from San Francisco shows why design matters: a 2019 study by Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade, and Franklin Qian found that the city’s rent-control expansion reduced tenant mobility, but landlords responded by converting some rental properties, contributing to a 15% reduction in the rental housing supply among affected properties.
That is a warning against rigid rules—not against all regulation.
Cities can limit annual increases while exempting new construction and allowing reasonable cost recovery.
Rent control is not a substitute for building housing; it is a tool to protect renters while supply catches up.
PRO concedes San Francisco's expansion exempted new construction and allowed cost recovery, yet Diamond, McQuade, and Qian still found a 15% rental-supply reduction.
That is not a design flaw; it is the predictable result of capping returns.
Cambridge's 1994 decontrol, studied by Autor, Palmer, and Pathak in 2014, raised property values and renovation, showing controls had suppressed maintenance.
Rent control misallocates units to long-tenured tenants and deters new rental construction.
Cities should instead expand housing supply, rental vouchers, and tenant protections.
The motion fails because even careful controls shrink the very housing it promises to protect.
The San Francisco study found a 15% decline among properties affected by the 1994 expansion—not a 15% fall in the city’s total rental supply.
Its authors also estimated that the policy’s displacement protections benefited incumbent tenants, underscoring the real trade-off: less mobility, but more stability.
Cambridge’s decontrol study found spillover increases in nearby property values; that does not establish that rent control should never be used.
Cities can pair limited, predictable increases with exemptions for new construction, maintenance allowances, and policies that expand housing.
Supply takes time to build; renters facing sharp increases need protection now.
PRO's defense narrows the harm without erasing it.
The 15% decline hit real rental units, and Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found landlords converted affected buildings, often to owner-occupied condos.
Incumbent stability was purchased by reducing homes available to newcomers.
Cambridge's decontrol raising values and renovation shows controls had discouraged upkeep.
"Predictable" caps still suppress returns; developers build where returns are uncapped.
Vouchers and tenant protections help renters without shrinking the rental stock.
Yes, supply takes time, but rent control makes that wait longer.
The motion asks cities to adopt a policy that, even carefully designed, contracts the housing it promises to protect.
The evidence supports caution, not a blanket rejection.
San Francisco’s 15% reduction applied to rental units in properties affected by its 1994 expansion, and Cambridge’s 1994 decontrol shows controls can discourage investment.
Cities should therefore adopt limited, temporary rent stabilization—not freeze rents—with new construction exempt, increases tied to inflation, and hardship increases available for documented costs.
That protects tenants from destabilizing spikes while preserving incentives to maintain and build housing.
Vouchers help eligible households, but they do not stop a sudden rent increase from displacing renters who need immediate protection.
Pair rent stabilization with more housing, and cities can address both urgent insecurity and long-term supply.
PRO's "limited, temporary" version still caps returns, and that is what drives the harm.
San Francisco's 1994 expansion exempted new construction, yet Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found a 15% rental-supply reduction among affected properties as landlords converted units.
Cambridge's 1994 decontrol raised property values and renovation, showing controls had suppressed upkeep.
Inflation-tied caps and discretionary hardship increases do not restore market returns; lenders underwrite future rent growth.
Temporary controls also create regulatory uncertainty that chills construction.
Vouchers and tenant protections help renters without shrinking the stock.
PRO has shown trade-offs, not a case for adoption.
Cities should adopt rent control to protect tenants from displacement, while expanding housing supply.
Diamond, McQuade, and Qian’s 2019 American Economic Review study of San Francisco’s 1994 expansion found that rent control reduced tenant displacement by 20 percent.
That is meaningful protection for people whose jobs, schools, and support networks depend on staying nearby.
The same study found affected landlords reduced rental housing supply by 15 percent, so design matters.
Cities should pair limits on increases for existing tenants with new-construction exemptions and more homebuilding.
Supply policy addresses scarcity; rent regulation protects residents while that supply arrives.
The same San Francisco study cuts against rent control.

Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found that while some tenants stayed, landlords responding to controls converted rental units to condos and TICs, cutting rental supply 15 percent and raising citywide rents by 5.1 percent.
Those gains went disproportionately to higher-income, older, and white tenants, not the vulnerable households the policy claims to protect.
Rent control also locks in misallocation: a tenant in a below-market unit cannot move without losing the subsidy.
Even with new-construction exemptions, existing stock shrinks.
Cities that want affordability should build, not cap prices.
The supply loss is real, but it does not erase the study’s displacement reduction.
Your distributional claim also omits an important finding: Diamond, McQuade, and Qian reported particularly strong displacement protection for racial minorities.
Building and tenant protection are complements, not substitutes: new housing cannot immediately protect someone facing a sharp rent increase today.
Design should address conversion incentives rather than ignore them.
Oregon’s 2019 law illustrates a less restrictive approach: it initially capped annual increases at 7 percent plus inflation and exempted buildings less than 15 years old.
Cities should adopt moderated protections alongside construction and anti-conversion measures, not freeze every rent indefinitely.
Your minority-protection point does not rescue the policy.

Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found the same expansion raised citywide rents by 5.1 percent, pushing costs onto unprotected renters—including younger, lower-income, and nonwhite households who lack rent-controlled units.
Even if some minority tenants stayed, the net effect is a regressive transfer.
Oregon’s cap is not moderate: in 2022 the CPI component allowed annual increases near 15 percent, yet it still discourages renovations and new supply because owners anticipate future controls.
Rather than layering anti-conversion rules on a failing price ceiling, cities should subsidize tenants directly and remove zoning barriers to building.
The 5.1 percent estimate is a serious warning, not proof that every rent-control design produces a regressive transfer.
The San Francisco study examined a particular expansion and landlords’ responses; it did not evaluate my proposed package of moderate caps, construction, and conversion restrictions.
Nor have you supplied evidence for your claim that Oregon’s new-construction exemption still discourages building.
I support tenant subsidies and zoning reform, but neither guarantees that an existing tenant can withstand a sudden increase.
The study’s 20 percent displacement reduction demonstrates a real benefit.
Cities should preserve that protection while addressing the documented supply risks, rather than abandon tenant stability.
You treat moderate caps as if they stay moderate, but Oregon’s inflation formula permitted 14.6 percent increases in 2023—hardly tenant protection.

The new-construction exemption only delays regulation; investors know legislatures can shrink or repeal exemptions later, as St. Paul’s 2021 3 percent cap showed when multifamily projects stalled until the council added a 20-year exemption.
Rent control’s 20 percent displacement benefit goes to current tenants, but future renters pay higher citywide rents and face fewer units.
Direct rental assistance can guarantee an existing tenant can stay without shrinking supply.
That is the better answer, not a system that protects some by making housing scarcer for others.
Governments should fund crewed missions alongside robotic ones because humans enable repairs, complex sample selection, and in-situ judgment that robots cannot match.

NASA’s Space Shuttle astronauts serviced the Hubble Space Telescope five times from 1993 to 2009, installing corrective optics and new instruments; without crewed repair, Hubble would have been a costly failure.
Apollo astronauts returned 382 kilograms of lunar samples with geological context, selecting diverse rocks that transformed planetary science.
Crewed stations like the ISS have also produced long-duration biomedical data essential for future exploration.
Robotic probes are valuable, but only human missions can test survival systems and adapt to unexpected findings in real time.
Crewed flight costs far more per unit of science, and the motion asks governments to fund it rather than rely on robots alone.
The Apollo program cost roughly $25 billion at the time, about 4 percent of the federal budget at its peak in 1966.
The ISS has cost well over $100 billion to build and operate.
Compare that with the Voyager probes, launched in 1977, which reached interstellar space and are still returning data.
Mars rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance have cost a few billion dollars each and carry out sophisticated geology.
Hubble's rescue also shows the problem: it needed repair only because the shuttle-era program was built around crew, and the Webb telescope operates at L2, far beyond crew reach, without servicing.
Limited budgets should buy the most discovery per dollar.
Cost per discovery is not the sole metric.
Webb cost nearly $10 billion and cannot be repaired or refueled at L2, while Hubble, upgraded by astronauts, has lasted over three decades and enabled Nobel-winning dark-energy work.
A few billion per rover overlooks that Perseverance drills slowly; Apollo crews collected 382 kg with geological context.
Crewed programs test life support, ISRU, and medical countermeasures no robot can.
Hubble’s flaw was a manufacturing error, not a crewed design; astronauts saved it.
Governments should not fund only robots; crewed capability is essential for deep-space science and future settlement.
Notice what my opponent's Webb point concedes: Webb needed no servicing, and it works.
Its success shows robotic design can deliver the science without a crew.

Hubble's Nobel-winning work was real, but the 2011 Nobel for dark energy rested on supernova surveys, much of it from ground telescopes, and Hubble's mirror flaw was a problem that crewed flight itself had to rescue, at the price of five shuttle missions.
Perseverance is slow, yet it is caching samples for return, and China's Chang'e-5 robotically returned about 1.7 kilograms of lunar material in 2020.
Life-support testing is a goal of crewed flight, not a scientific need.
If the aim is science, robots win per dollar; settlement is a separate value judgment that deserves its own debate.

My opponent misreads Webb: it works now but cannot be refueled or repaired, so its productive life is limited by propellant, while Hubble’s five crewed servicing missions extended it from a 15-year design life to over three decades.
The Nobel dark-energy result indeed used ground telescopes, but Hubble later provided crucial high-redshift data for cosmology.
Chang'e-5's 1.7 kilograms contrasts with Apollo crews' 382 kilograms and their contextual field geology; Perseverance has not yet returned anything.
Life-support research is not a mere goal—it is science in human physiology and enables the adaptable judgment that robotic probes lack.
Governments rightly fund capability and inspiration, not just the cheapest bit.
Webb's limited propellant is a fair point, but Webb carries roughly a decade or more of fuel, and the design choice to forgo servicing saved the cost of a crew-rated mission.
Hubble's extension also cost five shuttle flights, and the shuttle program itself ran well over $100 billion across its life.
That money could have launched many telescopes.
Apollo's 382 kilograms was real, but it came at about $25 billion in 1960s dollars, while Chang'e-5 returned its sample with one robotic mission.
Perseverance's cache awaits return, but that is a schedule issue, not proof robots cannot do it.
The motion asks governments to fund crewed missions; I say inspiration is worthwhile but not a scientific case, and budgets are finite.
Cities should charge drivers to enter their centres because scarce road space should not be free to congest.
London introduced its congestion charge in February 2003.
Transport for London’s first annual monitoring report found congestion within the charging zone fell by 30%, while traffic entering during charging hours fell by 18%.
Stockholm trialled congestion charging in 2006 and made it permanent in 2007.
These are implemented policies, not theoretical promises.
Charging also provides revenue that cities can invest in alternatives to driving.
The fair approach is to pair the fee with better public transport and targeted exemptions, not preserve congestion for everyone.
London's own record undercuts PRO.

Transport for London's later monitoring reports found that by 2006 and 2007 congestion in central London had climbed back toward pre-charge levels, as road space was reallocated to buses, cycling and roadworks.
Meanwhile the daily fee has tripled, from £5 in 2003 to £15 today.
A flat charge falls hardest on tradespeople, carers and low-paid shift workers who cannot choose when or how they travel, while the wealthy simply pay.
Voters understand this.
Edinburgh rejected a congestion charge in a 2005 referendum by roughly three to one, and Greater Manchester rejected one in 2008 by about four to one.
Better transit and smarter road management can cut traffic without pricing ordinary people out of their own city centres.
London’s rebound in congestion does not prove charging failed: reducing road capacity can increase delays even when fewer vehicles enter.
Your explanation itself identifies that distinction.
Nor do two rejected proposals establish universal opposition.
Stockholm’s September 2006 referendum produced 51.3% support for congestion charging, following its trial.
Distribution matters, but the answer is targeted relief, not free access for wealthy motorists too.
London provides a 100% congestion-charge discount for qualifying Blue Badge holders who register.
Cities should extend appropriate protections to essential journeys and invest revenue in alternatives.
Better transit and road management complement charging; they do not make scarce road space unlimited.
PRO concedes my point: London's congestion returned because of how road space was managed, not because of how many cars paid.
That shows road management decides congestion, so a permanent toll on ordinary drivers is the wrong lever.
On Stockholm, 51.3% is a bare majority, and several surrounding municipalities that held their own consultative votes rejected the charge, even though their residents pay it.
Edinburgh and Manchester voted by landslides against.
The Blue Badge discount helps disabled people, but it does nothing for the plumber, the home carer or the night-shift cleaner.
Each new exemption PRO proposes shows the fee is unfair to begin with.
Cities should fund transit openly, not by tolling people who have no alternative.
Road management affects congestion; it does not follow that traffic volume is irrelevant.
London’s initial 30% congestion reduction after charging is evidence against your claim that pricing is the wrong lever.
Stockholm’s 2006 trial reduced traffic crossing the charging cordon by about 22%.
These results matter more than whether one referendum majority was narrow.
Your strongest objection concerns people without alternatives.
That warrants targeted discounts and better transport, not abandoning a policy that reduces traffic.
Exemptions do not prove a policy inherently unfair; they make it fairer.
Cities should charge for scarce central road space while protecting essential access and funding alternatives.
PRO leans on early numbers, but London's 30% gain did not last.
TfL's own monitoring showed congestion back near pre-charge levels within a few years, while the fee kept rising.
A lever whose effect fades while its cost to drivers grows is a revenue tool, not a congestion cure.
PRO's answer to unfairness is ever more discounts, but every exemption weakens the traffic effect PRO depends on, so the policy is either unfair or ineffective.
Consent matters too.
In 2014, Gothenburg voters rejected their congestion tax by about 57% in a consultative referendum, and politicians kept it anyway.
Ordinary people deserve investment in transit and smarter streets, not a permanent toll imposed over their objections.
Rent control keeps families in their homes.
Oregon's 2019 law caps annual increases at 7% plus inflation; California's AB 1482 caps them at 5% plus inflation, max 10%.
St. Paul voters approved a 3% cap in 2021.
In San Francisco, economists Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found rent control increased tenant tenure and reduced displacement.
When rents spike, long-term residents, especially seniors and children, are pushed out, losing schools, jobs, and community.
Stability is a public good markets undersupply.
Rent control is a modest, tested tool to preserve it.
We can pair it with building more housing.
Vote PRO.
My opponent's own study undercuts the motion.

Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found that San Francisco landlords covered by the 1994 expansion of rent control cut the supply of rental housing they offered by 15 percent, converting units to condos and owner-occupied housing.
They estimated this pushed citywide rents up about 5 percent, harming the very future tenants rent control claims to protect.
St. Paul proves the point too: after its 2021 cap, residential permits fell sharply, and the city amended the law in 2022 to exempt new construction for twenty years.
A policy that must be gutted to keep builders working is no solution.
Build more housing instead.
Vote CON.
You concede the same study found rent control raised tenant tenure and cut displacement — the motion's core goal.
Its supply effect came from San Francisco's 1994 rule, which covered only pre-1980 buildings.
Oregon's 2019 law and California's AB 1482 exempt housing under 15 years old, severing that conversion channel; St. Paul's 2022 change is the same design fix, not a repeal.
And "build instead" doesn't house this year's evictee: construction takes years and still rents at market.
Stability and supply together beat supply alone.
The conversion channel isn't severed; it's intact.
Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found the supply loss came from landlords of existing covered buildings converting them, and Oregon's and California's caps cover exactly such existing buildings.
Exempting new construction protects builders, not the older rental stock that renters depend on.
And tenure isn't the same as fairness.
The authors themselves argued rent control works like a tax on landlords that falls on whichever tenants happen to be in place, regardless of need.
The tenant who stays benefits, while the next family pays higher rents.
If the goal is to keep this year's evictee housed, emergency rental assistance and housing vouchers target need directly without shrinking supply.
Vote CON.
CON says vouchers target need directly.
In practice, HUD reports only about one in four eligible households gets federal rental assistance, and waiting lists run years.
Rent control reaches every renter automatically.
The same Diamond study found tenure gains concentrated among older, long-tenured tenants, those least able to absorb a spike.
And San Francisco's conversion channel ran through condo-conversion and owner-move-in rules cities can restrict, not the cap itself.
Oregon and California exempt fifteen years of new housing, so building continues.
Stability plus supply is the practical path.
Vote PRO.
My opponent's strongest point is that only about one in four eligible households gets federal rental assistance.
But that is a funding choice we can fix, not a reason to adopt a policy that reaches every renter "automatically," including affluent tenants who need no help, while new arrivals pay more.
Restricting conversions doesn't solve the problem either.
Landlords keep cutting maintenance and redeveloping, and blocking every exit just freezes a shrinking stock.
Cambridge, Massachusetts offers evidence: Autor, Palmer, and Pathak found that after voters ended rent control in 1994, property values and investment rose in both decontrolled and nearby buildings.
Stability funded by everyone, targeted at need, beats stability charged to whichever landlord you happen to rent from.
Vote CON.
Robotic probes are superb scouts, but only crews adapt in real time.
In 1993 shuttle astronauts repaired Hubble's flawed optics; later servicing missions installed new cameras and gyroscopes, yielding decades of science no robot could then match.
The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000, enabling long-duration human research—bone loss, radiation, fluid shifts—that informs Mars plans.
Apollo 11's 1969 landing and twelve moonwalkers inspired a generation.
Governments fund crews not instead of robots but because humans improvise and because citizens support what they see people risk.
Cutting crews to robots alone cedes leadership to China's Tiangong station.
The question is not whether astronauts can do valuable work; it is whether governments should prioritize crewed missions over robotic exploration.
Crews require life support, radiation protection, and safe return systems, adding risks and costs that robots avoid.
Meanwhile, robotic missions have delivered major science: NASA’s Perseverance rover landed on Mars in 2021, and OSIRIS-REx returned an asteroid sample to Earth in 2023.
Human research aboard the ISS is useful, but it does not prove that sending people to Mars is safe or necessary.
Governments should fund missions for what they can discover, not assume that a human presence is worth its additional expense.
You say robots avoid risk, but Perseverance and OSIRIS-REx succeed at tasks designed years ahead; they cannot repair a jammed drill or replace a failed instrument.
Hubble proves the difference: in 1993 astronauts corrected its mirror, and later shuttle crews installed new cameras, extending its life decades.

Your Mars-safety standard is backwards: ISS crews since 2000 have given us bone-loss and radiation data, the very evidence needed; you cannot require proof before funding the missions that produce it.
Governments fund crews because citizens back visible risk, and because retreat cedes low Earth orbit to China's Tiangong.

Hubble shows that astronauts can perform repairs, not that crewed missions are the best use of exploration funds: NASA’s 1993 servicing mission required the Space Shuttle, a crew, and a purpose-built repair campaign.
Perseverance and OSIRIS-REx, by contrast, delivered major results without risking astronauts.
Nor does ISS experience settle the Mars radiation question: the station orbits within Earth’s magnetosphere, while crews travelling to Mars would spend substantial time beyond it.
And leadership need not mean putting people in orbit; robotic missions can build scientific capability without making a crewed presence the measure of national success.
You are right that ISS sits inside the magnetosphere; that is why we must go beyond it.
Artemis I in 2022 flew instrumented mannequins past low Earth orbit to measure deep-space radiation.
Long-duration physiology still comes from ISS crews.
Apollo 17's geologist Harrison Schmitt, in 1972, spotted orange volcanic soil that robots had not; field judgment matters.
Funding crews does not cancel Perseverance; the motion rejects robotic-only.
And China keeps Tiangong crewed continuously since June 2022; a robotic-only America would watch.
Governments fund crews because citizens back visible risk, not line items.
Artemis I measured radiation on one uncrewed lunar flight; it did not establish that long-duration Mars exposure is safe.
Schmitt’s field observation shows that trained humans can notice things robots miss, not that crewed missions are the most effective way to fund discovery.
Robots can be designed to investigate promising finds, and they avoid putting astronauts at risk.
Nor does Tiangong make a crewed program essential to leadership: China’s presence is a political argument, not proof that the scientific return justifies the cost.
The motion asks governments to fund crews rather than only robots; scarce budgets should favor missions that deliver science without requiring human life support and safe return.
The four-day week has been tested, and it works.
In Britain's 2022 pilot, 61 companies and roughly 2,900 employees cut hours with no cut in pay for six months.
Afterward, 56 of those 61 firms kept the policy.
Sick days fell about 65 percent and resignations dropped 57 percent, while revenue held steady and rose slightly on average.
Iceland's public-sector trials from 2015 to 2019 covered about 2,500 workers, and researchers found productivity maintained or improved in most workplaces.
Microsoft Japan reported a 40 percent jump in sales per employee during its 2019 trial.
Burnout is expensive and turnover is expensive.
A shorter week makes companies leaner, healthier and more attractive to talent.
The pilot evidence is weaker than it looks, and it does not justify a general move by companies.
Start with selection.
The 2022 UK pilot, run by 4 Day Week Global, recruited firms that volunteered.
Companies eager to try a shorter week are the ones most likely to succeed at it, so the results cannot be projected onto the economy at large.
Those 61 firms were also a small, mostly small-business sample, many in services and professional work, where output is easiest to compress.
There was no control group, and the self-reported revenue figures cover only six months.
Microsoft Japan's 40 percent figure compared sales per employee in a single August against the previous August, a short-term snapshot.
Sectors with fixed coverage needs, such as hospitals, factories, retail and customer service, cannot simply compress hours without hiring more staff, which raises costs.
Whether a four-day week suits a firm should be negotiated, not adopted as a general standard.
My opponent says volunteers skew results, but the motion asks companies to move toward this, and the evidence shows that firms which try it overwhelmingly keep it.
A follow-up a year after Britain's pilot found that 54 of the 61 companies still ran a four-day week, and 31 had made it permanent.
That is no six-month snapshot.
On fixed-coverage sectors, Iceland's trials included preschools, social services and hospitals, where staff reorganized shifts rather than simply working fewer hours.
Coverage is a scheduling problem, not a wall.
Staggered rotas keep doors open while each worker gets three days off.
Negotiation firm by firm is exactly how this transition should happen, and the direction should be four days.
My opponent's follow-up statistic confirms the selection problem rather than answering it.
Firms that volunteer, get consultancy support from the organizers, and choose to continue are self-selected twice over, so a 54-of-61 retention rate says little about firms that were never keen.
Iceland is also weaker support than it sounds.
Those trials were public-sector, where the taxpayer absorbs costs, and some workers reported higher pressure to compress tasks into fewer days.
Staggered rotas keep doors open, but covering five or seven days with workers who each put in fewer hours requires more people or more overtime, which costs money.
Where output can't be compressed, a four-day week at full pay is a raise.
My opponent concedes negotiation is the right path, which undercuts the motion's call for companies to move generally.
Selection cuts both ways.
Every workplace reform, from the weekend itself to remote work, began with volunteers, and nobody argues pioneers' success proves nothing.
What matters is whether results hold as adoption spreads, and Iceland answers that.
After its trials, unions negotiated shorter hours, and by 2021 roughly 86 percent of Iceland's workforce had moved to shorter hours or gained the right to.
That is scale, not a hand-picked few.
On cost, my opponent ignores the other side of the ledger: Britain's pilot saw resignations drop 57 percent and sick days fall about 65 percent, and replacing staff is expensive.
I never conceded the destination.
Negotiation is the method; four days is the goal.
Vote PRO.
My opponent's Iceland claim needs care.
The roughly 86 percent figure describes workers who gained shorter hours or the right to them, and those new contracts typically cut the week from 40 to about 35 or 36 hours.
That is a modest trim, not a four-day week, so Iceland does not show that the model scales.
It also followed public-sector trials where the taxpayer carried the cost.

Fund both—but rejecting crewed missions as redundant is wrong.

NASA's inspector general estimated in 2022 that each early Artemis launch costs about 4.1 billion dollars, more than an entire Curiosity mission.
And no human has left low Earth orbit since Apollo 17 in 1972, while robots kept going.
Cassini orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, New Horizons flew past Pluto in 2015, and Chang'e 6 sampled the lunar far side, where no crew has ever landed.
JWST's lack of repair access is a design trade, and it has worked superbly anyway.
Insight comes from reaching more places.
Robots reach more places, for less money, without risking a single life.
Rent control is a proven tool to stop displacement and stabilize communities.
In San Francisco, a 2019 study by Stanford economists found that rent-controlled tenants were 20 percent more likely to remain in their homes, shielding them from eviction and neighborhood churn.
Voters in St. Paul, Minnesota, approved a 3 percent annual cap in 2021, and Oregon’s 2019 statewide law limits increases to 7 percent plus inflation.
Berlin’s 2020 rent freeze covered roughly 1.5 million apartments before being overturned by courts.
These policies give working families certainty about housing costs, which is essential when wages lag behind market rents.
PRO's own Stanford study, by Diamond, McQuade and Qian, cuts the other way.
It found landlords subject to San Francisco's 1994 expansion of rent control reduced their rental housing supply by 15 percent, converting units to condos and owner-occupied housing.
That lost supply raised citywide rents by about 5 percent, harming the very renters the policy meant to protect.
St. Paul proves the point too.
After its 2021 cap, residential permits dropped sharply, and in 2022 the city council exempted new construction for 20 years.
Berlin's freeze, struck down in 2021, coincided with a steep fall in advertised rental listings.
Rent control helps incumbents at the expense of newcomers and future supply.

My opponent leans on the Diamond-McQuade-Qian paper, but that same study found rent-controlled tenants in San Francisco were 20 percent more likely to stay and received aggregate benefits of $2.9 billion from 1995 to 2012.
The 15 percent supply reduction came mostly through condo conversion under California’s Costa-Hawkins loopholes, not rent control itself.
Modern laws avoid that: Oregon exempts buildings under 15 years old, and St. Paul’s 2022 amendment exempted new construction for 20 years.
Berlin’s listing drop coincided with a court challenge and pandemic, not a controlled experiment.
Policy design, not the principle, determines supply effects.
PRO's numbers concede my case.
The same Diamond-McQuade-Qian paper estimated that the citywide rent increases caused by lost supply imposed costs on renters roughly equal to the $2.9 billion in benefits to protected tenants.
That is a transfer from newcomers to incumbents, not a net gain.
Condo conversion was not a loophole.
It was landlords' direct response to rent control, using exits like the Ellis Act.
PRO's "better design" also proves my point.
Oregon exempts buildings under 15 years old, and St. Paul exempted new construction for 20 years, because both conceded that controls deter building.
A policy that works only when it excludes new housing does not solve a housing shortage.
Cities need more supply.
You concede the central fact: $2.9 billion in tenant gains from San Francisco’s 1995–2012 rent control experience.
Calling that a mere transfer misses what the same study found: protected tenants stayed 20 percent longer, avoiding eviction, school moves, and job loss.
Supply losses came from Ellis Act condo exits under a 1994 expansion, not from modern policy design.
Oregon’s 15-year and St. Paul’s 20-year exemptions for new construction are not admissions of failure; they target controls at current tenants while preserving incentives to build.
That is the right two-part strategy: protect renters now and add supply for the future.
PRO calls the $2.9 billion a central fact I concede, but the Diamond-McQuade-Qian paper estimated rent control's citywide rent increase cost other renters about $2.9 billion too.
The gains PRO celebrates were paid for by other renters.
PRO also says the supply losses came from Ellis Act exits, "not rent control."
But the Ellis Act was passed in 1985.
Landlords used it after 1994 because rent control gave them a reason to leave the rental market.
Any city adopting controls faces that same response.
Finally, exempting new construction for 15 or 20 years only delays the problem.
Builders know exemptions can be repealed, and older buildings still shrink.
Subsidies and zoning reform help renters without shrinking supply.
London's congestion charge, launched in 2003, cut traffic in the charging zone by about 15 percent and congestion by roughly 30 percent in its first year, while bus ridership rose.
Stockholm's 2006 congestion tax, made permanent in 2007, reduced traffic into the central cordon by around 20 percent and increased public transport use, cutting air pollution in the inner city.
Milan's Area C, begun in 2012, reduced vehicle entries by about 30 percent.
These pricing schemes curb emissions, fund transit, and return street space to people.
Cities should follow this evidence.
Those early gains are real, but they fade and they come with costs the motion ignores.
London's own transport authority found that congestion in the zone returned to roughly pre-charge levels within a few years, even as the charge rose from £5 to £15 by 2020.
Traffic speeds in central London are now about as slow as before 2003, partly because road space was reallocated and private-hire vehicles multiplied.
A flat fee is also regressive: it asks a nurse driving a night shift to pay the same as a banker, while wealthier drivers simply absorb it.
Cities can reduce traffic through better transit, parking policy, and targeted low-emission rules without taxing access to the centre, where shops and workers depend on customers arriving.
My opponent mistakes slower speeds for failed pricing.

London still has roughly one fifth fewer vehicles entering the charging zone than before 2003; congestion worsened partly because road space was reallocated to buses and cycling and private-hire vehicles multiplied.
Stockholm’s cordon traffic remains about 20 percent lower a decade after its tax began.
The nurse example backfires: London’s charge operates only 07:00–18:00 on weekdays, so night-shift drivers pay nothing.
Resident discounts and disabled exemptions ease fairness, and net revenues—over £1.5 billion by 2019—fund buses and roads.
Pricing plus reinvestment is more equitable than letting cars choke centres.
My opponent concedes my central point: London's speeds are back to pre-charge levels, and the explanation is that road space was reallocated and private-hire vehicles multiplied.
A fee that cannot hold congestion down once the city changes around it is a weak tool.
I accept the night-shift correction; the charge runs on weekdays only in daytime.
But the fairness problem remains for early-shift cleaners, carers, tradespeople with tools, and anyone whose job lacks a decent transit route.
Exemptions help residents, yet they create their own boundary disputes and loopholes.
Revenue is not proof of success either, since it measures how many people still pay.
Drivers with the least flexibility pay most, and the wealthy simply absorb the charge.
Better bus networks and parking limits achieve much of this without a toll.
My opponent mistakes a single metric—speed—for the policy’s purpose.
A fee that cuts total vehicle entries, even when speeds later recover, still reduces emissions, noise, crashes, and street space taken by cars.
London’s charging zone sees roughly one fifth fewer vehicles than before 2003, and Stockholm’s cordon traffic remains about 20 percent lower.
Fairness is answered by time-limited hours, resident and disability exemptions, and reinvestment in buses and cycle routes that serve early-shift workers.
Parking limits and bus improvements help, but only a price signal shifts daily travel choices while raising dedicated revenue that the wealthy also pay into.
PRO now defends the fee by its vehicle counts, so let me meet that.

Fewer cars entering is a real gain, but London's own reviews attributed much of the later improvement in air quality to the Ultra Low Emission Zone, a targeted emissions rule, not the congestion charge.
That supports my case: cities can regulate pollution directly without charging for access.
And a fee tuned to cut traffic is a poor fit for a goal like cleaner air, since it taxes a clean electric car's presence the same as a dirty one, unless the city adds exemptions and complexity.
Where buses are poor, drivers have no alternative and simply pay.
Build the alternatives first, and target the pollution itself.
Governments should fund crewed missions because humans can adapt, repair, and make judgments no robot can.

NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990 with a flawed mirror; five space shuttle servicing missions between 1993 and 2009 installed corrective optics and new instruments, turning a near-failure into one of history’s most productive observatories.
Apollo astronauts returned 382 kilograms of Moon rocks from 1969 to 1972, enabling decades of laboratory analysis, while robotic sample returns have been far smaller.
Crewed missions also generate public support and engineering skills that a robotic-only program cannot sustain.
This is not a choice against robots; it adds irreplaceable capability.
Hubble shows that humans can repair hardware in orbit, not that governments should prioritize crewed missions over robotic ones.
The five servicing missions required the Space Shuttle, whose final flight was in 2011; NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope instead operates at Sun–Earth L2, where astronauts cannot service it.
Robots can also return samples: NASA’s OSIRIS-REx delivered material from asteroid Bennu to Earth in 2023, and Japan’s Hayabusa2 returned samples from Ryugu in 2020.
Crewed missions add life-support systems, launch mass, and serious risk to people.
Governments should fund them only when their distinct benefits justify those costs—not make human presence a default condition for exploration.
Your Hubble example is not an exception but evidence of a general advantage.

Five crewed servicing missions extended Hubble's life and upgraded instruments over three decades, while JWST at L2 is unrepairable by design—a choice made only after crewed servicing capability was discarded.
Robotic sample returns have yielded grams: Hayabusa2 returned 5.4 grams, OSIRIS-REx over one hundred grams.
Apollo returned 382 kilograms, collected in real time by a trained geologist, not a preprogrammed scoop.
Human judgment, adaptability, and public inspiration are distinct benefits that justify the cost.
Funding crewed missions preserves the option for future servicing and deeper exploration.

Apollo’s 382 kilograms of lunar samples do not show that crewed missions are the best use of exploration funds: the Moon is a nearby, accessible target, while Hayabusa2 and OSIRIS-REx returned asteroid material from far greater distances without risking astronauts.
Their returns—5.4 grams and 121.6 grams, respectively—were scientifically valuable.
Nor does JWST’s location at Sun–Earth L2 prove that robotic exploration followed the abandonment of servicing; it shows that a mission can be designed to operate there without crews.
Human adaptability is real, but preserving that option does not justify making crewed missions a funding priority over robotic science.
Your examples of distant robotic sample returns show that robots can gather small amounts of material safely, but they do not show that crewed missions should be defunded.

The International Space Station, occupied since 2000, has required hundreds of astronaut spacewalks for assembly, repair, and upgrades—tasks no robotic arm has yet performed autonomously under real conditions.
Apollo returned 382 kilograms of lunar rock precisely because a trained geologist could select diverse samples on the spot, something a preprogrammed scoop cannot match.

Robots and crews are complementary, but the unique judgment, dexterity, and adaptability of people justify government funding for crewed flight, especially as we prepare for sustained lunar and martian operations.
Cost and risk are real, yet the distinct benefits are not available any other way.
The ISS shows that astronauts can do difficult work in orbit; it does not show that governments should prioritize crewed exploration over robotic missions.
The ISS has depended on robotic systems too, including Canadarm2, which has supported assembly and maintenance since 2001.
And lunar sample selection is not limited to humans: NASA’s Perseverance rover has collected and cached Martian rock samples for a planned return mission.
Crewed missions demand life support and expose people to hazards that robots avoid.

Governments should fund human spaceflight when a specific objective warrants those costs, but robotic missions should remain the priority when they can answer the scientific question more safely and affordably.
Governments should fund crewed missions alongside robotic ones, not instead of them.

NASA astronauts repaired and upgraded the Hubble Space Telescope during five servicing missions between 1993 and 2009, extending its working life and improving its instruments—work no robot then performed.
Apollo astronauts also brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil for study on Earth.
Robots are essential for reaching dangerous or distant places, but people can respond flexibly to unexpected findings and maintain complex equipment.
A space program that funds only robots gives up those capabilities, and the scientific opportunities they can create.
Robotic missions deliver more science per dollar than crewed ones.

NASA’s Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity operated for years for about 820 million dollars total, while the Apollo program cost roughly 25 billion in 1960s dollars and returned only a few hundred kilograms of rock.
Japan’s Hayabusa2 and NASA’s OSIRIS-REx returned asteroid samples robotically at a fraction of any crewed mission cost.
Crewed flight requires life support, food, water, and heavy radiation shielding, which consume mass and funds without improving scientific instruments.
Humans also face bone loss and radiation damage on long flights.
Given limited budgets, governments should fund only robotic missions to maximize discovery and avoid risking lives.
The robotic sample returns prove that robots are valuable, not that governments should fund only robots.

OSIRIS-REx returned 121.6 grams from asteroid Bennu; Apollo astronauts brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar samples, which researchers can examine with techniques unavailable at the time of collection.
Those missions pursued different goals, so comparing their costs as if they bought the same science is misleading.
Crewed missions also repaired and upgraded Hubble, including replacing its flawed optics in 1993.
Human spaceflight carries real risks and costs, but abandoning it would surrender capabilities robots have not fully replaced.
Your comparison of sample masses misses the point.
The question is what a fixed budget buys in scientific knowledge, not grams returned.

Apollo cost roughly 25 billion dollars in 1960s money, an enormous sum, while robotic missions like Hayabusa2 and OSIRIS-REx return material from distinct asteroids for far less and with no risk to life.
The 1993 Hubble repair is history; it does not prove today's robotic servicing could not do similar tasks.
Funding should follow current capability, not nostalgia.
Crewed flight has not yielded a unique scientific result robots could not obtain.
Robots maximize science per dollar.
A fixed budget matters, but “science per dollar” is not the only public benefit, and the claim that crewed flight has produced no unique results is too strong.
Apollo astronauts collected samples in geologically varied locations and documented context in real time; those observations helped scientists interpret the samples.
Robots can do more each year, but Hubble’s five astronaut servicing missions show that humans have already repaired and upgraded a complex observatory in orbit.
Governments should weigh that adaptability and the knowledge gained from human exploration against cost and risk—not prohibit crewed missions outright.
Funding both approaches preserves options as capabilities change.
You say science per dollar is not the only benefit, but the motion is about government funding priorities.
Public inspiration is not unique to crewed flight; robotic images from Mars and deep space also engage millions.

The claim that crewed flight produced unique results rests on Apollo's context, yet modern orbiters and rovers document geological context with high-resolution cameras and spectrometers without risking lives.
Hubble's 1993 repair is a single historical case; no current law requires human hands for such tasks.
Given scarce budgets, funding robots rather than crewed missions maximizes documented scientific return and avoids the huge costs of life support and safety.
Cities should charge drivers to enter their centres because scarce road space should not be free when its use delays everyone else.
London introduced congestion charging in February 2003.
Transport for London’s first annual monitoring report recorded a 30% reduction in congestion and a 15% reduction in traffic circulating within the charging zone compared with 2002.
That is practical evidence, not merely economic theory.
The fee should fund better public transport, with targeted exemptions for people who genuinely need to drive.
The alternative—rationing access through traffic jams—charges everyone in wasted time while raising nothing to improve travel.
Charging entry fees is regressive: a nurse on a night shift pays the same as a banker, regardless of income or alternatives.
It penalises residents just inside the zone and businesses dependent on car-borne customers, while traffic is simply displaced to surrounding roads, raising pollution there.
Durham’s congestion charge, introduced in 2002, was scrapped in 2011 because it cost more to run than it raised.
Instead of taxing access, cities should improve bus and rail frequency, expand cycling networks, and use smarter traffic signals.
These measures cut congestion without pricing lower-income workers out of their own city.
Your fairness objection supports targeted relief, not abandoning charging.
London residents within the zone can receive a 90% discount, and its weekday charging hours are 7am to 6pm: a night-shift nurse does not necessarily pay.
Displacement is not inevitable: Transport for London’s first annual monitoring report found no significant increase in traffic on roads outside the zone attributable to charging.
Stockholm’s 2006 trial reduced traffic crossing its charging cordon by about 22%.
Better buses and cycling are essential, but charging complements them by reducing competing car traffic and providing revenue.
Free entry is not fair when bus passengers bear drivers’ congestion costs.
Your resident discount only shifts the burden onto the lowest-paid non-residents.
A hospital cleaner who starts a 7 a.m. shift inside the zone pays the full fee, while a wealthier flat-owner inside it pays almost nothing.
That is not fairness; it is income-blind pricing that leaves nurses on early shifts and suburban care workers exposed.
Nor is displacement settled: later London reviews found rising congestion on boundary roads just outside the charging zone, even if the first annual report did not highlight it.
Stockholm’s 22% cut measures fewer cars, not which trips were lost—often flexible trips by poorer drivers, not the banker’s commute.
Your cleaner example exposes a design problem, not a case against charging: relief should follow income and transport need, rather than residence alone.
Starting work at 7 a.m. also does not establish that a cleaner enters the zone during charging hours.
Boundary congestion deserves monitoring, but rising congestion alone does not prove charging caused it.
Likewise, Stockholm’s traffic reduction does not establish that poorer drivers disproportionately abandoned trips; that requires evidence about travellers’ incomes.
Stockholm made congestion charging permanent in August 2007 after its trial and referendum.
Cities should combine charging with targeted relief and better public transport, not preserve congestion as their allocation system.
Calling it a design problem does not rescue the motion as written.
Real schemes do not offer income-based relief: London’s 90% discount is residence-based, and Stockholm’s charge varies by time, not by the driver’s income.
Verifying income at every entry would require pre-registration or refund claims, which poorer drivers are least able to complete.
A cleaner arriving at 8 a.m. for a 9 a.m. shift pays the same as a company director, and no major scheme has solved that.
If fairness requires redesigning the policy this heavily, then the unqualified motion—charge drivers to enter centres—should be rejected.
Companies should move to a four-day week with no loss of pay, testing shorter hours rather than squeezing five days into four.
In the UK’s 2022 trial, 61 companies involving approximately 2,900 workers tried this approach for six months.
Afterwards, 56 companies chose to continue, including 18 that confirmed the change was permanent.
The evaluation, involving researchers at the University of Cambridge and Boston College, reported that 71% of employees experienced reduced burnout.
This was not a universal or randomized experiment, but it demonstrates practical feasibility.
Companies should judge work by results, not by how many days employees occupy a desk.
The UK pilot shows that some self-selected employers can make a shorter week work; it does not establish that companies generally should adopt one.
The trial was voluntary, lasted six months, and had no randomized control group, so its results cannot show that the schedule caused the reported benefits or would transfer across industries.
A four-day week with unchanged pay also raises hourly labor costs by 25% if output and staffing stay constant: 32 paid hours instead of 40.
That may be manageable in some office jobs, but not where customers need coverage every day or output depends on staffed hours.
Companies should choose based on their operations, not adopt a universal rule.
Your methodological caution is fair, but a 25% increase in hourly pay is not automatically a 25% increase in cost per unit produced.
That depends on productivity.
In the UK pilot, revenue remained broadly unchanged among the 23 organizations supplying comparable data, rising 1.4% on average, weighted by company size.
Coverage also need not mean everyone takes Friday off: companies can stagger rest days.
These findings do not prove universal suitability, but they justify moving toward shorter weeks through measured trials.
Where staffing requirements prevent immediate adoption, implementation should adapt to operations rather than dismiss the goal.
Staggering days off can preserve five-day coverage, but it does not remove the need to staff the same hours with fewer hours per employee.
In round-the-clock or customer-facing operations, that may require extra hires, overtime, or reduced service—costs a company cannot solve merely by measuring results differently.
And the revenue figure comes from only 23 organizations that supplied comparable data, in a voluntary six-month trial; unchanged revenue is not proof of unchanged profit or higher productivity.
The UK pilot supports testing the model where it fits, not a general move by companies.
Employers should retain the choice to set schedules that meet their operational needs.
You are right that revenue is not profit, and continuous coverage can require additional staffing.
But coverage concerns do not establish that shorter hours are impractical.
Iceland’s 2015–2019 public-sector trials involved about 2,500 workers, including shift workers, reducing weekly hours to 35 or 36 without cutting pay.
The evaluation reported that productivity and service provision remained unchanged or improved in most participating workplaces.
That is not proof that every company can adopt 32 hours immediately.
It supports a phased move: test shorter hours, track costs and service, and retain successful changes.
Operational differences should shape implementation, not rule out the goal.

Iceland’s trials do not settle the case for a company-wide four-day week: they tested public-sector reductions to 35 or 36 hours, not a universal 32-hour schedule, and public services differ from businesses facing direct competition and profit constraints.
The sensible conclusion is to let employers test schedules where staffing, costs, and service allow—not to urge companies generally to move to four days.
A phased trial is a management option, not proof that the goal should be adopted across companies.
Retaining that choice protects workers and customers from a schedule that may fit some workplaces but not others.
Cities should charge drivers to enter their centres because it works.
London's congestion charge began in 2003 at £5; Transport for London reported traffic entering the zone fell about 15% and congestion dropped sharply.
Stockholm's 2006 trial cut traffic across the cordon by roughly 20%, and voters kept the tax in 2007.
Singapore has charged since 1975.
Milan's Area C, launched in 2012, reduced traffic and PM10.
Charges also raise revenue for buses and cycling.
Driving into a crowded centre imposes costs on everyone; pricing makes drivers face them, cutting jams, emissions and journey times.
Congestion pricing is a flat tax that hits lower-income drivers hardest: a £15 daily charge is a far larger share of a cleaner's wage than a banker's.
Stockholm's cordon pushed some traffic onto surrounding roads, increasing jams and pollution just outside the zone.
Milan's Area C gives residents deep discounts, shifting costs to outsiders and delivery vans.
Enforcement and camera systems consume a big slice of revenue; London spends tens of millions each year just running the charge.
Cities should instead expand bus lanes, cycle networks and coordinated traffic signals, which cut jams without pricing poorer residents out of their jobs.
A flat fee is regressive, but the revenue isn't: Stockholm's charge funds public transport, and London gives zone residents a 90% discount.
Lower-income Londoners are far less likely to drive into the centre; they gain from faster buses.
Displacement is real but modest, and Stockholm's monitoring found net congestion and emissions fell after the trial.
Enforcement costs exist, yet the scheme still raises substantial net revenue for transit.
If costs are high, improve technology; don't scrap a proven tool.
Bus lanes alone don't price road space—without a charge, traffic rebounds and fills the space you free.

Your resident discount is not progressive: London's 90% discount applies only to residents inside the cordon, some of Europe's most expensive postcodes, not to poorer drivers in outer boroughs who must cross the zone for shift work.
Saying lower-income people don't drive ignores cleaners, carers and tradespeople.
Stockholm's surrounding roads saw increased congestion, and residents there pay with worse air.
The net revenue after cameras and enforcement is far smaller than the headline charge; London's scheme yields modest net funding for buses.
And if the fee works, it falls; if it doesn't, it's just a toll on the poor.
We need better buses, not a charge.
You call it a toll on the poor, but Stockholm's trial paired the charge with 197 new buses and expanded park-and-ride, and bus ridership rose; carless lower-income residents gained.
Outer-borough drivers aren't charged unless they enter the centre.
Stockholm's monitoring found net congestion and emissions fell across the county, despite some local displacement.
London's net revenue still funds buses and cycling.
And your "if it works, it falls" point is backwards: falling traffic is success, letting cities cut the fee or reinvest.
Better buses alone don't manage demand; pricing plus transit does.
Your transit pairing proves my point: if 197 new buses and park-and-ride did the heavy lifting, build those first and skip the toll.
Charging before alternatives exist simply fines shift workers who cannot change routes or hours.
Outer-borough drivers are not optional entrants; many are carers and cleaners crossing the cordon because jobs are there.
County-wide averages hide real harm: Stockholm’s own monitoring recorded increased congestion on some approach roads, and those residents breathe it.
London’s net revenue after camera and enforcement costs is modest, not a transit fund.
Declining traffic is not success when it comes from pricing out poorer drivers rather than giving them a real choice.
Road space in a city centre is scarce and valuable, yet most cities give it away for free, and the predictable result is gridlock.
Congestion charging fixes this by putting a price on the scarce resource.
Singapore pioneered it in 1975 with its Area Licensing Scheme and moved to electronic road pricing in 1998.
London introduced its congestion charge in February 2003, and Transport for London reported that congestion within the zone fell by about 30 percent in the early years.
Stockholm ran a trial in 2006 that cut traffic across its cordon by roughly 20 percent, and voters then backed making it permanent.
New York began charging in January 2025.
Charging works, and the revenue can fund better public transport.
The motion treats driving as a luxury, but for many low-paid workers—cleaners, care workers, night-shift staff—a car is the only option because buses and trains don't run when they work.
London's congestion charge is not income-based: a banker and a hospital porter both pay the same £15 daily fee.
That is plainly unfair.
Charging also hurts small shops inside the zone, as customers drive to edge-of-town malls instead, emptying the very centres the fee claims to protect.
Before taxing drivers, cities should fund better buses, safer cycle routes, and flexible work hours—not price out the poor.
My opponent's night-shift worker is largely untouched by charging.
London's charge applies only from 7am to 6pm on weekdays and noon to 6pm at weekends, so most night shifts fall outside it, and residents inside the zone get a 90 percent discount.
More fundamentally, the poorest commuters into central London overwhelmingly take buses and trains, not cars.
A free road subsidises the drivers, who are typically better off, while bus passengers sit in their traffic.
Charging speeds up buses, and under the Greater London Authority Act 1999 the revenue must be spent on transport.
On shops, a 2009 study by Daunfeldt and colleagues found Stockholm's charge had no significant effect on inner-city retail.
Funding better buses and charging work best together.
Your night-shift defence is too narrow: the charge also covers weekday 7am starts and weekend noon starts, hitting cleaners and carers arriving for morning or midday shifts.
The 90 percent resident discount helps wealthy residents, not low-paid workers who cannot afford to live inside the zone and commute from outer boroughs.
You claim poor commuters use buses, but that is because they are priced out of driving; some still must drive because buses do not cover their routes or times.
Stockholm’s 2009 study is not generalisable: central Stockholm has high tourism and wealth, unlike many industrial cities.
A flat fee remains regressive wherever alternatives are poor.
My opponent concedes the core point: the poorest commuters already ride buses.
That is exactly why charging is progressive.
It takes a fee from drivers, who are on average better off, and London law requires that revenue to be reinvested in transport, so the people stuck in traffic on buses benefit.
Where some workers still need cars, the answer is targeted exemptions.
London already exempts Blue Badge holders.
Abolishing the policy would only keep everyone in gridlock.
On generalisability, charging is not just for wealthy tourist capitals.
Gothenburg, an industrial port city, introduced a congestion tax in 2013, and small Durham has charged since 2002.
Free roads are the real regressive subsidy.
Conceding that poor commuters use buses does not make a flat fee progressive; it ignores poor workers who must drive because bus routes or shift times fail them.
A £15 charge takes a far larger share of a cleaner’s wage than a banker’s, and Blue Badge exemptions do not cover that.
Reinvesting revenue helps bus riders, not the driver who paid and still has no alternative.
Durham’s £2 charge covers one historic street, not a city centre, and Gothenburg’s tax funded a specific rail tunnel package, not general traffic reduction.
These are not generalisable.
Rent control protects something markets price poorly: stability.
Families who lose leases lose schools, jobs, and community ties, and eviction is strongly linked to poverty, as Matthew Desmond documented in Evicted.
The strongest modern evidence supports this protective effect.

Stanford economists Diamond, McQuade and Qian studied San Francisco's 1994 expansion of rent control and found covered tenants were substantially more likely to remain at their addresses years later, especially older and longtime residents.
Critics cite the same study's finding that some landlords converted units.
That problem calls for better design, not abandonment.
Oregon showed how in 2019 with statewide rent stabilization, capping annual increases at 7 percent plus inflation and exempting new construction to protect building incentives.
Rent control transfers stability from future renters to current ones, but it shrinks the very housing it regulates.

The Stanford study PRO cites also found San Francisco’s 1994 expansion cut rental housing supply by 15 percent and raised citywide rents by 5.1 percent, as landlords converted to condos or left the market.
Those costs fall on newcomers, the young, and lower-income families, who face higher prices and fewer vacancies.
Oregon’s 2019 cap exempts new construction, but most existing tenants still receive below-market protection, discouraging maintenance and mobility.
A better policy is direct housing vouchers, which help poor households without reducing supply.
CON's numbers come from conversions, not from rent control itself.
Diamond, McQuade and Qian attribute the 15 percent supply drop among treated buildings largely to landlords converting units to condos and owner-occupancy.
That is a loophole, and cities can close it with conversion limits and replacement requirements.
The authors themselves suggest policy could be redesigned to avoid these supply losses.
Vouchers cannot replace stabilization.
Housing Choice Vouchers are not an entitlement, and the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates only about one in four eligible households receives federal rental assistance.
Vouchers also do nothing about sudden rent spikes for middle-income tenants.
Stability for the families living in a city now is a legitimate public goal, not a theft from newcomers.
PRO’s loophole fix underestimates supply damage.
Diamond et al. found the 15 percent supply loss came not only from condo conversion but from landlords selling to owner-occupants and redeveloping.
California’s Ellis Act lets owners leave the rental market, and local conversion limits cannot override that state right.
Banning conversions may push owners to sales, evictions, or neglect, while replacement requirements make new construction more expensive.
On vouchers, PRO admits only one in four eligible households receives aid; that is a funding choice, not a design flaw.
Expanding direct vouchers helps poor renters without raising citywide rents or reducing supply, unlike rent control, which also gives subsidies to high-income sitting tenants.
CON's Ellis Act point actually proves mine.
That supply loss stems from a specific California state law, not from rent control as such.

Cities elsewhere, and states like Oregon, can design stabilization without that exit ramp, and New York's 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act tightened the rules that had let landlords pull units out of regulation.
Vouchers are no free lunch either.
Scott Susin's 2002 study found that vouchers raised rents for low-income households who did not receive them.
Calling the one-in-four coverage gap "a funding choice" concedes that the aid poor renters need does not exist today.
Rent stabilization protects tenants now, at little public cost, and cities should adopt it.
PRO is right that the Ellis Act is California-specific, but that does not save rent control.

In Cambridge, Massachusetts, rent control ended in 1995, and Autor, Palmer and Pathak found its removal increased rental supply and improved building quality, while the controls had reduced available units and raised rents for uncontrolled tenants.
No conversion loophole was needed.
