“Move toward” need not mean a universal schedule; it means treating a shorter week as a serious option and redesigning work where coverage and results allow it.
Your employer-by-employer flexibility is compatible with that direction, but it does not explain why companies should reject it as a goal.

The UK pilot’s self-selection limits how widely we can generalize, yet 56 of 61 participating organizations continued after the trial—a concrete reason to take the model seriously, not proof that every sector should copy it.
Companies should pursue the benefits where feasible, measure outcomes, and adapt or decline where they are not.
PRO's final position is that companies should treat a shorter week as a serious option, pursue it where feasible, and decline where not.
That is a description of what rational firms already do, not a case for the motion.
If every firm should simply weigh the option and decide, then "should move to a four-day week" is the wrong resolution, and the affirmative has conceded the point.
The evidence remains narrow.
The UK pilot ran six months with volunteers, and Iceland's trials covered public-sector workplaces.
Neither tested shift-based work at scale, where cutting a day means hiring more staff or paying overtime.
I urge a vote against the motion as written.
Robots are invaluable, but a space program without humans gives up capabilities no machine has matched.
Consider Hubble.

Launched in 1990 with a flawed primary mirror, it was rescued in 1993 by astronauts on a Space Shuttle servicing mission, and four later crewed missions upgraded it, extending its scientific life by decades.
Consider Apollo: six crewed landings returned about 382 kilograms of lunar samples, while the Soviet robotic Luna missions returned roughly 300 grams.
Apollo 17 carried a trained geologist, Harrison Schmitt, who recognized orange volcanic glass on the spot.
The International Space Station, continuously crewed since November 2000, is the only laboratory studying how human bodies endure spaceflight.
Our future depends on that knowledge.
Hubble’s rescue demonstrates astronauts’ usefulness, not that crewed missions are the best public investment.

NASA’s inspector general projected in 2021 that Artemis would cost $93 billion through fiscal year 2025, with production and operations costing $4.1 billion per SLS/Orion launch for the first four missions.
Robots avoid life-support requirements and risks to crews.
NASA’s OSIRIS-REx returned 121.6 grams from asteroid Bennu in 2023, without astronauts.
Apollo’s larger sample haul does not establish better value per dollar.
Studying human adaptation to space is valuable chiefly if we choose to send humans; it cannot independently justify that choice.
My opponent treats this as crewed versus robotic, but the motion only asks that governments not fund robots alone.
Both can coexist, and they reinforce each other: astronauts serviced Hubble, a robotic telescope, five times.
On cost, NASA's entire budget in fiscal 2023 was about $25 billion, well under one percent of federal spending.
Robotic missions are not cheap either: Perseverance cost roughly $2.7 billion and still cannot improvise, repair itself, or choose samples the way Schmitt did.
On circularity, humans have already chosen to live in space; the ISS has hosted people continuously for over two decades.
Abandoning crewed flight would throw away that hard-won knowledge just as other nations, including China with its Tiangong station, expand theirs.
Coexistence does not erase opportunity costs: funding astronauts still competes with other public priorities.
NASA’s small share of federal spending does not establish that crewed missions deliver good value.
Hubble’s servicing was impressive, but Webb began science operations in 2022 without astronaut assembly or servicing.
Robots also surpass your Soviet sample-return benchmark: China’s Chang’e 5 returned 1,731 grams of lunar material in 2020.
Perseverance’s limitations do not make life support, crew transport, and rescue requirements disappear.
Finally, ending continuous occupation would not erase published ISS research.
Past expenditure and China’s choices are not sufficient reasons for governments to keep financing crewed flight.
My opponent's best examples actually support funding both.
Webb cost about $10 billion and sits roughly 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, beyond any repair.
Its engineers counted 344 single-point failures during deployment, and any one of them could have ended the mission.
Hubble, serviced by astronauts, has now worked for over three decades.
Chang'e 5's 1,731 grams is impressive, yet Apollo returned over two hundred times more.
And China, my opponent's robotic champion, funds crewed flight alongside it, operating Tiangong and planning crewed lunar landings.
Spacefaring nations treat the two as complements.
Opportunity cost is real, but a capability that repairs, improvises, and explores deserves part of a small budget.
Vote PRO.
Webb’s deployment risks were real, but it deployed successfully without astronauts.
Its distance illustrates why crewed repair is not a general solution; Hubble’s accessibility was exceptional.
Apollo’s sample mass proves capacity, not cost-effectiveness, and China’s spending choices do not establish public value.
The question is not whether astronauts can contribute, but whether their additional capabilities justify their additional expense and risk.
NASA’s inspector general estimated $4.1 billion per launch for the first four SLS/Orion missions, excluding development costs.
Governments should fund scientific results, not assume human presence is indispensable.
Your examples establish usefulness, not a compelling case for public funding.
Rent control protects something markets don't price: stability.
When rents spike, families are uprooted, children change schools, and older tenants lose the neighborhoods they built.

The best-known modern study, by Stanford economists Diamond, McQuade and Qian in 2019, found that San Francisco's 1994 expansion of rent control made covered tenants significantly more likely to stay at their addresses, with the strongest effects among older and longer-term residents.
That is the policy working as intended.
Modern rent stabilization is not a crude freeze.
Oregon in 2019 and California through AB 1482 capped annual increases while still allowing rents to rise with inflation.
Cities should adopt this kind of moderate, inflation-indexed protection for renters.
PRO cites Diamond et al., but that same 2019 study found San Francisco's rent control cut rental housing supply by roughly 15 percent, as landlords converted units to condos or owner-occupancy.
Benefits went to incumbents; newcomers faced a tighter market and higher rents.
Oregon's 2019 cap and California's AB 1482 exempt new construction precisely because builders stop building under caps.
Economists from Assar Lindbeck to Paul Krugman have criticized rent control for reducing housing quantity and quality.
Moderate or not, caps discourage maintenance, create shortages, and ration housing by luck rather than need.
CON is right that Diamond, McQuade and Qian found treated landlords reduced rental supply by about 15 percent.
But look at how: mainly by converting buildings to condos and owner-occupied housing.
That is an enforceable loophole, not an iron law, and cities can restrict conversions alongside caps.
CON's second point actually supports my case.
Oregon exempts buildings for their first 15 years, and AB 1482 exempts buildings for 15 years on a rolling basis.
Builders keep building because new units are not covered, while existing tenants are protected from sudden spikes.
As for "rationing by luck," eviction by price spike rations housing by wealth.
I think stability for incumbents, especially older renters, is worth defending.
You say conversion is a loophole cities can close.

San Francisco already restricts condo conversions, yet its 1979 ordinance's 1994 expansion still shrank rental supply; owners took units off-market via owner-move-in evictions, which caps don't prevent.
And the very exemptions you praise are concessions that building cannot survive under caps, which is why Oregon and AB 1482 exclude 15-year-new units; the controlled sector still shrinks.
Krugman's 2000 Times column: rent control "has done more harm than good," reducing supply and creating decay.
Stability purchased by shrinking the pie is still rationing.
CON says San Francisco's restrictions failed, but much of that supply loss runs through state law cities couldn't change.
California's 1985 Ellis Act lets landlords exit the rental business entirely, and the 1995 Costa-Hawkins Act bars vacancy control and exempts newer units from local caps.
That is evidence that rent control needs complete design, not that it can't work.
Owner-move-in evictions can be policed with residency verification and relocation payments.
And exempting new construction is not a confession of failure; it is smart design that protects builders and tenants at once.
Shrinking supply is a real cost, but displacing elderly renters is also a cost.
Moderate, well-enforced stabilization is worth adopting.
Blame Ellis and Costa-Hawkins all you like; they are the law cities actually face.
A city cannot override them, so the "complete design" you promise is unavailable, and the measured harms persist.

Diamond, McQuade and Qian found the 1994 expansion cut rental supply about 15 percent and raised citywide rents; exemptions for new buildings do not restore the older controlled stock, which still ages and exits.
Residency checks and relocation payments police one exit route, not condo conversion, demolition, or landlord exit.
Krugman's 2000 verdict stands: rent control has "done more harm than good."
Stability for some incumbents is not worth shrinking housing for everyone else.
Cities should adopt rent control because it keeps families housed.
In St. Paul, Minnesota, voters in 2021 capped annual increases at 3 percent.
Oregon in 2019 set a statewide limit of 7 percent plus inflation, preventing sudden rent shocks.
A Stanford study of San Francisco’s rent control found it raised the probability that a tenant stayed in their home by 20 percent.
That stability benefits schools, jobs, and local businesses.
Opponents warn of reduced supply, but moderate caps like St. Paul’s still allow landlords predictable returns.
The alternative—unchecked rent hikes—displaces families and deepens homelessness.
Rent control is not a cure-all, but it is a proven stabilization tool.
Rent control helps those who already hold apartments and hurts everyone else.

The Stanford study PRO cites, by Diamond, McQuade and Qian (2019), also found that after San Francisco expanded rent control in 1994, landlords of affected buildings cut rental housing supply by 15 percent, by converting to condos or redeveloping.
The authors concluded this likely drove up citywide rents, offsetting the benefit to tenants.
St. Paul's 3 percent cap, passed in November 2021, was followed by a sharp drop in building permits, and the city amended it in 2022 to exempt new construction for 20 years.
That correction shows the original design discouraged building.
Stability for some, paid for by scarcity for newcomers, is a poor trade.
Cities should build more housing instead.
Your own example proves the case for smart rent control, not against it.
St. Paul amended its cap to exempt new construction for 20 years, and Oregon’s 2019 law already exempts new buildings for 15 years.
That directly answers the Diamond study’s finding: San Francisco’s 1994 rules lacked such exemptions, so landlords converted units.
When cities exempt new supply, rent control protects current tenants without discouraging building.
The permit drop you cite may also reflect the 2021–22 pandemic construction slowdown, not the cap alone.
Stability and new housing can coexist.
Cities should adopt rent control with new-construction exemptions—not reject the tool outright.
PRO's fix concedes my point: the original designs were harmful enough that both St. Paul and Oregon had to carve out new construction.
But the exemption does not cure the Diamond finding, which concerned existing buildings.
Landlords of controlled units converted them to condos and redevelopments, shrinking the rental stock.
A new-construction exemption does nothing to stop that.
St. Paul's amendment also left the 3 percent cap on existing units, with no allowance for rent resetting between tenants.
Exempting new buildings is also a standing gamble that the exemption survives, since developers know a future council can end it.
The pandemic does not explain St. Paul's drop, because Minneapolis, with no cap, saw permits keep rising.
Better to expand supply and give vouchers to those at risk.
Your objections describe one badly designed law, not rent control itself.
San Francisco’s 1994 expansion lacked strong anti-conversion rules; modern ordinances can limit condo conversion of controlled units and require replacement rentals upon demolition.
New-construction exemptions in Oregon (15 years) and St. Paul (20 years) are statutory, not fleeting council whims, and a city council cannot overturn a state law.
California’s statewide cap allows vacancy resets, preserving turnover and maintenance incentives.
Minneapolis’s permit rise followed its 2040 upzoning and metro growth, so the comparison is not clean.
Rent control should pair with supply policies; stability for current tenants need not sacrifice future housing.
PRO now says rent control must be bundled with anti-conversion rules, replacement requirements, vacancy resets, and upzoning.
That is a concession that rent control alone does not work.
If the supply policies do the work, cities should adopt those and skip the cap.
Vacancy decontrol also cuts against PRO's stability case, since it lets landlords push out tenants to reset rents.
Oregon's law is statewide, which is exactly why a city cannot rely on it.
Even Diamond's authors found that tenants benefited while the city as a whole lost, because rents rose citywide.
A tool that needs this many patches is a poor default for cities.
Cities should adopt rent control as a guardrail against sudden rent hikes that can uproot residents, while exempting new construction and allowing reasonable increases.
Oregon’s 2019 law offers one model: it limits annual increases in covered homes and exempts buildings less than 15 years old.
Rent control is not a substitute for building more housing; it protects tenants while cities work to expand supply.
A 2019 study of San Francisco found rent control helped covered tenants stay in their homes, but also that landlords reduced rental supply.
That is a warning to design the policy carefully—not a reason to leave renters wholly exposed.
My opponent's own evidence undercuts the motion.

The 2019 Stanford study by Diamond, McQuade and Qian found that San Francisco landlords subject to rent control cut their rental supply by 15 percent, converting units to condos and owner-occupied housing, and that this pushed citywide rents up about 5 percent.
Rent control protected the lucky incumbents while making the city costlier for everyone searching for a home.
St. Paul shows the same danger: after voters passed strict rent control in 2021, residential permits fell sharply, and the city soon amended it to exempt new construction for 20 years.
The better cure is more supply, plus targeted vouchers for struggling tenants.
The San Francisco study identifies a real tradeoff, not proof that every rent-control design raises rents citywide.

Oregon’s 2019 law limits covered annual increases to 7% plus inflation and exempts buildings less than 15 years old—protecting existing tenants while preserving a stronger incentive to build new housing.
St. Paul likewise amended its 2021 policy to exempt new construction for 20 years; that change shows cities can adjust rules when supply concerns arise.
More housing and targeted vouchers matter, but they do not stop a sudden rent increase from displacing a tenant today.
Rent control is a useful, carefully designed protection alongside those policies.
My opponent's defense creates a dilemma.
Oregon's cap is so loose it barely bites: with high inflation, the 2023 limit reached 14.6 percent, and the legislature then had to cap it at 10 percent.
A tenant facing a 10 percent hike is hardly protected from displacement.
Make the cap tight enough to matter, and you get San Francisco, where the supply losses came from existing buildings converted to condos.
Exempting new construction does nothing to stop that.
St. Paul's amendment came after the damage to permits had already happened, which shows the policy has real costs.
For sudden hikes, emergency rental assistance helps the tenant without shrinking the housing stock.

A 10% cap is not complete protection, but it limits how far a covered tenant’s rent can jump; emergency assistance helps only tenants who qualify and receive it, and does not itself stop a landlord from raising rent.
San Francisco’s supply loss is a serious warning, not a verdict on every policy: cities can exempt new construction and revise rules when evidence shows harm.
The choice is not rent control or more housing.
Cities should build more and provide targeted aid, while giving existing tenants a predictable limit on rent hikes that could otherwise force them from their homes.
My opponent concedes the core problem: a cap loose enough to avoid harm, like Oregon's, barely protects anyone, while a cap tight enough to matter invites San Francisco's outcome.

"Revise rules when evidence shows harm" means waiting until units are already lost, and in San Francisco that harm came from existing buildings converted to condos, which no new-construction exemption prevents.
Those conversions displaced tenants too, so rent control can cause the very uprooting it promises to stop.
Assistance does not limit landlords, true, but it does not shrink supply either, and it reaches tenants by need rather than by luck of tenure.
When economists across the spectrum largely reject rent control, cities should build, subsidize, and vote no.
Cities should adopt rent control to protect tenants from displacement, while preserving incentives to build.
Diamond, McQuade, and Qian’s 2019 American Economic Review study of San Francisco found that rent control reduced tenant displacement by 20 percent.
That is a concrete benefit: more residents could remain in their homes.
The same study found that affected landlords reduced rental supply by 15 percent, so design matters.
Cities should pair limits on rent increases with new-construction exemptions and additional housing development.
Rent control is not a substitute for building homes; it is protection for existing tenants while cities address shortages.
PRO's own source undercuts the case.

Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found that landlords subject to San Francisco's 1994 expansion cut rental supply by 15 percent, largely by converting units to condos and owner-occupied housing, and they estimated this pushed up citywide rents by about 5 percent.
That is a transfer from future renters and newcomers to incumbent tenants, and the study's authors concluded the policy likely fueled the gentrification it aimed to prevent.
PRO promises new-construction exemptions, but St. Paul shows the risk.
Voters there passed a strict 3 percent cap in 2021, residential permit applications fell sharply, and the city amended the law in 2022 to exempt new construction.
Targeted housing vouchers protect tenants without shrinking supply.
The San Francisco supply loss is a serious objection, not a reason to ignore the study’s 20 percent reduction in displacement.
New-construction exemptions alone are insufficient: cities should also address conversions that remove regulated rentals.
St. Paul’s initial policy lacked that exemption; its 2022 amendment supports adopting safeguards from the outset, rather than repeating its design.
Vouchers are valuable, but they require funding and do not themselves create homes.
Congress funds federal housing vouchers; cities cannot simply guarantee them to every threatened tenant.
The better approach combines rent stabilization, rental-stock preservation, vouchers, and construction—not a choice between tenant protection and supply.
PRO now concedes that exemptions are insufficient and proposes adding conversion bans, but that admits rent control's distortions require ever more regulation to contain.
San Francisco already restricted condo conversions, yet landlords still removed units through redevelopment and other conversions.
Meanwhile the displacement benefit PRO cites went to incumbent tenants, while everyone searching for housing faced higher rents.

Economists broadly agree: in the 2012 IGM Forum survey, most leading economists rejected the claim that rent limits in New York and San Francisco had improved the amount and quality of affordable housing, and almost none agreed.
PRO says vouchers need funding, but so does any real solution.
Rent control simply hides its cost in reduced supply.
Means-tested assistance targets need rather than tenure.
The IGM survey addressed whether rent controls improved the quantity and quality of affordable housing, not whether protecting tenants from displacement matters.
I accept the supply objection; I reject treating it as the only outcome.
Diamond, McQuade, and Qian found both reduced displacement and reduced rental supply.
That evidence supports safeguards, not pretending the tenant benefit disappears.
Means-tested assistance targets income, but without adequate funding it offers no guarantee against a sudden rent increase.
Cities should adopt rent stabilization with new-construction exemptions, monitor rental-stock losses, and expand housing.
The goal is tenant stability alongside supply growth, not rent control instead of construction.
PRO concedes the core problem: rent control shrinks supply.
The IGM survey's scope doesn't rescue the policy, because displacement protection bought with fewer rental homes simply shifts displacement onto the next family priced out.
Diamond, McQuade, and Qian themselves suggested that government-financed subsidies could protect tenants without discouraging rental supply.
Cambridge, Massachusetts offers further evidence.
After voters ended rent control there in 1994, Autor, Palmer, and Pathak found that decontrol raised property values and spurred investment in the housing stock.
PRO's answer to every distortion is another rule, plus monitoring.
A simpler path protects stability better: build more, fund targeted emergency rental assistance, and help households by need, not by how long they've held a lease.
Vote CON.
Cities should adopt rent control to protect tenants from displacement, while expanding housing supply.
Diamond, McQuade, and Qian’s 2019 American Economic Review study of San Francisco found that rent control reduced tenant mobility by 20 percent and lowered displacement from the city.
It also found landlords reduced rental supply by 15 percent—a real cost, not a reason to disregard tenant security.
The sensible response is targeted rent stabilization paired with construction and protections against rental conversion.
Predictable rent increases give existing tenants a better chance to remain in their homes; housing expansion addresses scarcity.
Cities need both.
Rent control doesn't add housing; it taxes new supply.
The same San Francisco study PRO cites found landlords cut rental supply 15 percent and converted units to condos, pushing citywide rents up.
Existing tenants win lotteries while everyone else pays more.
Berlin's 2020 rent freeze coincided with a sharp drop in advertised rentals before courts struck it down in 2021.
Cambridge, Massachusetts abandoned rent control in 1994; economists widely agree controls deter construction and maintenance.
If cities want affordability, they should build more and expand vouchers, not cap rents.
The San Francisco supply loss is real, but “taxes new supply” is not true of every design.
Oregon’s 2019 rent-stabilization law exempts buildings less than 15 years old.
Cities can likewise protect new construction while limiting increases in older housing.
Berlin’s freeze was struck down in 2021 because the state lacked legislative authority, not because the court established that rent regulation cannot work.
Your alternatives also leave current tenants exposed while construction takes time.
The San Francisco study found reduced displacement among protected tenants.
That benefit matters.
Adopt stabilization with new-construction exemptions and safeguards against conversion, alongside more building and vouchers.
You're right that Oregon exempts buildings under 15 years, but the tax still falls on older units, exactly where San Francisco landlords cut rental supply 15 percent and converted to condos.
Berlin's court ruling was about state authority, yet advertised rentals fell sharply during its freeze.
Your design still creates lottery winners and losers: protected tenants stay, but the San Francisco study found citywide rents rose, hurting unprotected renters.
Building and vouchers expand supply for everyone; rent caps ration existing stock.
That is why Cambridge abandoned controls in 1994.
Protect tenants with direct subsidies, not price ceilings.
Your supply objection is serious, but vouchers do not themselves create housing, and construction does not immediately protect sitting tenants.
San Francisco’s results show both reduced displacement and reduced rental supply; they justify safeguards, not ignoring either outcome.
Oregon’s exemption for buildings less than 15 years old demonstrates that stabilization need not cap rents in newly built housing.
I support limits on increases during tenancies, paired with new-construction exemptions, conversion protections, more building, and subsidies.
No policy eliminates scarcity overnight.
Cities should protect current tenants against displacement while addressing supply, rather than make tenant security wait for construction.
PRO now concedes the 15% supply cut.
Exempting new buildings does not spare older stock, where San Francisco landlords converted units and reduced rentals.
Oregon's 15-year exemption just delays the tax.
Vouchers don't build, but neither do price caps; caps ration existing units and create lottery winners while unprotected renters face higher rents.
Direct subsidies can be delivered now and paired with construction.
Cambridge scrapped controls in 1994, and Berlin's freeze saw advertised rentals fall before courts voided it in 2021.
Tenant security achieved by shrinking the rental market is not security.
Build, subsidize, and protect—don't cap.
Cities should charge drivers to enter their centres because road space is scarce and currently rationed by delay.
Congestion pricing replaces that with a visible price, and the evidence is strong.
Stockholm's charge, made permanent after a 2006 trial, cut traffic across the cordon by roughly 20 percent and has kept it down.
London's charge, launched in 2003, reduced traffic in the zone substantially at first.
Singapore has priced roads since 1975.
New York began its central business district toll in January 2025, and early data showed fewer vehicles entering and faster trips for many commuters.
The revenue can fund buses, trains, and safer streets, so the policy cuts pollution, crashes, and gridlock while paying for alternatives.
A fee may reduce traffic, but it makes access depend more on ability to pay than need.
London’s congestion charge began in 2003 at £5 per day; that price has since risen substantially.
People who cannot afford to live near work may have few practical alternatives to driving, especially where public transport is poor.
Nor does less traffic guarantee less congestion: Transport for London reported that congestion in the charging zone rose after the scheme’s initial years, amid roadworks and changes to road capacity.
Cities should improve transit and manage roadworks first.
A charge can raise money, but it should not be treated as a reliable or fair substitute for those measures.
My opponent's equity worry is real, but the data cut the other way.
In central London and Manhattan, most commuters already travel by transit, and drivers entering the core are disproportionately higher-income.
In Manhattan's central business district, roughly 90 percent of workers commute by means other than driving.
So free road space is the regressive default: many poorer people on buses subsidize the few who drive.
Pricing can also fund discounts, and New York offers low-income driver discounts and tax credits for some residents.
On London, I concede congestion rose after the early years.
But TfL attributed much of that to roadworks and street redesign for bus and cycle lanes, not to the charge failing.
Without the charge, traffic would likely have been worse.
Transit investment and pricing work together, because the revenue pays for the transit.
A 90-percent transit commute share does not show that the remaining drivers can switch modes, or that every trip is discretionary.
New York’s low-income discount illustrates the gap: eligible drivers receive a 50-percent discount only after their first 10 trips in a month, so occasional trips get no discount.
And a driver-based measure of fairness misses people who must travel for care, disability-related needs or work in areas with poor transit.
Revenue for better buses may help later, but it does not make today’s charge affordable or create an alternative where none exists.
Cities should provide viable alternatives before charging people to reach essential destinations.
My opponent is right that some trips cannot be shifted, but that is an argument for exemptions, not for free road space.
New York exempts qualifying vehicles carrying people with disabilities, and the toll applies once per day, so a single essential trip costs one charge.
Most drivers have options: Stockholm's traffic fell about 20 percent without any collapse in access to the centre, which suggests many trips were flexible.
"Alternatives first" also sets an impossible sequence.
Transit expansion costs billions, and the toll is what pays for it; New York's was designed to fund roughly $15 billion in capital work.
Waiting leaves gridlock, pollution and crashes in place.
Charge, exempt the vulnerable, and reinvest.
Exemptions do not solve the broader problem: eligibility rules can miss people whose work, caring duties or location leave them no practical alternative.
Nor does a fall in Stockholm traffic prove access was unaffected for every group; it shows fewer vehicles crossed the cordon.
New York’s toll began in January 2025, so its planned $15 billion in capital funding is not the same as transit improvements already available to drivers paying today.
Cities should first make reliable alternatives accessible across neighbourhoods, then consider pricing with protections tested in advance.
Charging before that risks turning an infrastructure gap into a fee on essential travel.

Iceland ran the world’s largest four-day week trial from 2015 to 2019, covering about 2,500 workers, and found productivity stayed the same or improved in most workplaces while wellbeing rose sharply.
Microsoft Japan tested a four-day week in August 2019 and measured a 40 percent jump in productivity per employee, alongside lower electricity use.
A 2022 UK pilot involving 61 companies reported that most firms kept the policy after the trial ended.
These are not hypothetical gains.
Companies that move to four days often retain staff longer, cut burnout, and lose little or no output.
The trials you cite are small and self-selected.
Iceland's 2,500 workers were mostly public-sector employees with flexible tasks, roughly 1% of the workforce.
Microsoft Japan's one-month summer experiment lacked a control group.
The UK pilot's 61 firms were mostly small, not representative of large employers.
The Information Technology and Innovation Foundation argued in 2023 that cutting hours without cutting pay raises unit labor costs, which many firms cannot absorb.
Hospitals, factories, and shops need continuous coverage; a four-day week would force expensive overhiring or reduced service.
Scaling these niche successes economy-wide is not proven.
Small, self-selected trials are not a flaw; they show which workplaces can adopt the model without harm, and voluntary adoption is what the motion proposes.
Your unit labor cost concern assumes output falls when hours fall.
Iceland found productivity stayed the same or improved, so costs per unit did not rise.
Microsoft Japan’s 40 percent gain is not proof for every firm, but it refutes the claim that less time must mean less output.
Continuous coverage is solved by staggering four-day schedules, as nurses and factory shifts do.
In the 2022 UK pilot, 56 of 61 companies continued after six months, not because they were forced, but because it worked.
Staggering does not make coverage free.
If a ward or factory line runs seven days, cutting each worker to four days requires roughly 25 percent more staff, or four ten-hour days, which is not a shorter week.
Iceland's trials were mostly public-sector, not a template for continuous manufacturing.
The UK pilot's 56 continuing firms survived six months, but many were small and few resembled large manufacturers with fixed costs.
The 2023 ITIF analysis still holds: with pay unchanged and output unable to rise, unit labor costs climb.
A voluntary niche is not a case that companies should move.
Your staggering objection presumes output is locked to hours.
In services, finance, and administration, much of the day leaks into meetings and presenteeism, not produced units.
When those hours go, output can hold or rise without extra staff.
The February 2023 UK pilot report found revenue broadly maintained or increased, sick days down 65 percent, resignations down 57 percent across its 61 firms.
Atom Bank, a regulated UK lender, made its four-day week permanent after a 2021 trial and kept service while attrition fell.
The ITIF analysis only bites if output is fixed; trials show it is not.
That is the working case for moving.
Your examples are real but still service-sector and self-selected.
The UK pilot’s 61 firms and Atom Bank prove some offices can cut presenteeism; they do not prove hospitals, logistics, or factories can.
There, coverage is the product, so a fourth day off means hiring more staff or extending shifts to ten hours, not a four-day week.
The ITIF analysis stands for fixed-output settings: same pay, same required coverage, fewer hours means higher unit labor costs.
A voluntary niche is not a general mandate.
The motion says companies should move; most cannot without raising costs or cutting service.
Cities should adopt rent control because housing is not an ordinary good: families cannot easily relocate without losing jobs, schools, and community.

Stanford economists Diamond, McQuade, and Qian studied San Francisco's 1994 expansion of rent control and found it reduced tenant displacement; covered tenants were about 10 to 20 percent more likely to stay at their address.
That stability matters most for elderly and low-income renters.
Modern rent stabilization, like Oregon's 2019 statewide cap of 7 percent plus inflation, does not freeze rents; it limits sudden spikes while allowing reasonable increases.
Tenants facing a 30 percent hike have no real bargaining power.
Rent regulation protects them from that shock.
My opponent cites the right study, but it cuts against them.

Diamond, McQuade and Qian found that San Francisco landlords subject to the 1994 expansion reduced the supply of rental housing they offered by 15 percent, converting buildings to condos and owner-occupied units.
The authors estimate this pushed citywide rents up about 5 percent, costing future renters roughly as much as current tenants gained.
Rent control protects whoever holds a lease today and taxes everyone searching tomorrow: young workers, newcomers, the poor who must move.
Oregon's cap shows the alternative.
Targeted help like housing vouchers, plus permission to build more homes, protects vulnerable tenants without shrinking supply.
My opponent's account of the Stanford study is accurate, and I accept it.
But it measures a 1994 policy that covered only small multifamily buildings built before 1980, while exempting newer construction.
That is the design flaw, not an indictment of regulation.
Modern laws, like Oregon's 2019 statute, exempt buildings for their first 15 years, so new construction is not discouraged.
Conversions to condos are curbed by limits in many ordinances.
The study also confirms my core point: tenants stayed in their homes, and the authors noted the policy served as insurance against rent increases.
Vouchers and building more are worthwhile, but vouchers are not an entitlement, and construction takes years.
Tenants facing spikes today need protection now.
Exemptions don't rescue rent control.
They concede the core problem.
If regulation didn't deter building, no new-construction exemption would be needed.
St. Paul learned this in 2021.
Voters passed a strict 3 percent cap with no exemption, building permits fell sharply, and the city amended the law in 2022 to exempt new construction for 20 years.
Limits on condo conversion are no fix either.
San Francisco already restricted conversions, yet controlled supply still fell 15 percent as landlords redeveloped or occupied units themselves.
And Oregon's cap of 7 percent plus inflation rarely binds, so it offers little protection.
For urgent help, emergency rental assistance targets need now without shrinking tomorrow's housing.
My opponent's Oregon point actually helps me.
If a 7 percent plus inflation cap rarely binds, then it costs landlords little while still blocking the extreme spikes that cause displacement.
That is the case for moderate stabilization: insurance against shocks, not a price freeze.
The St. Paul episode shows a badly drafted law, a strict 3 percent cap with no exemption, was fixed within a year.
That is good policy design responding to evidence, not proof that all regulation fails.
Even the Stanford authors found rent control delivered large benefits to the tenants it covered, who stayed in their homes.
Emergency assistance is funded year to year; a cap protects tenants now, at no cost to the treasury.
Cities should adopt well-designed stabilization.
My opponent's defense has become a contradiction.
A cap that rarely binds protects almost no one.
A cap that does bind triggers the supply losses the Stanford study measured.
Oregon shows this: when inflation surged, the formula allowed 14.6 percent increases for 2023, and lawmakers then imposed a hard 10 percent ceiling.
The cap kept tightening, as caps do.
Nor is rent control free.
Its cost simply moves off the budget and onto future renters, through the roughly 5 percent citywide rent increase the Stanford authors estimated.
St. Paul's quick "fix" was itself an admission that caps deter construction.
Cities should fund targeted assistance and legalize building, not adopt rent control.
Cities should adopt rent control because housing is not an ordinary good: moving is costly, and a sudden rent hike can uproot families, children's schooling, and entire communities.
Modern rent stabilization, which caps annual increases rather than freezing rents, protects tenants without banning profit.
Oregon passed a statewide cap in 2019, limiting annual increases to 7 percent plus inflation.
Stanford economist Rebecca Diamond's study of San Francisco found rent control reduced displacement of covered tenants, keeping them in their homes and neighborhoods.
Critics rightly note it can reduce rental supply, but well-designed policies exempt new construction, preserving incentives to build.
Stability is a public good, and cities should deliver it.
PRO cites Diamond's San Francisco study but omits its main finding: rent control reduced rental housing supply by 15 percent and raised rents in uncontrolled units by 5 percent.
Protecting some tenants means fewer apartments for everyone else.
Oregon's 2019 cap of 7 percent plus inflation is not rent control in the traditional sense; it still allows large increases.
St. Paul, Minnesota adopted a strict 3 percent cap in 2021, and after new apartment permits collapsed, it had to exempt new construction within a year.
Well-designed policy is not immune: any cap discourages maintenance and new supply.
Cities should not adopt rent control.
Con is right that Diamond found supply effects, and I concede them.
Her study covered San Francisco's 1994 expansion to small multifamily buildings, and landlords of those buildings converted units or redeveloped, cutting rental supply about 15 percent.
But that is a flaw in a design that covered older small buildings without protecting against conversion, not proof that all stabilization fails.
Her study also found tenants were 10 to 20 percent more likely to stay at their address, and the benefits to them were large.
St. Paul actually supports my point: it amended the ordinance to exempt new construction, which is the design I advocated.
Cities can learn, and tenants deserve protection while they do.
PRO argues San Francisco’s 15 percent supply loss was a design flaw, not inherent to rent control.
But the mechanism matters: landlords of existing rent-controlled units converted to condos, moved in owners, or demolished, because caps cut returns.
Exempting new construction does nothing to preserve that older stock, which is precisely where affordable apartments sit.
St. Paul’s experience is not a vindication.
After its 2021 3 percent cap, new apartment permits collapsed, forcing the council to exempt new buildings in 2022.
Even then, developers faced policy uncertainty.
Rent control’s harms come from the cap itself, not from missing exemptions, and cities should not adopt it.
Con says the harm comes from the cap itself, but the evidence points to design.
Diamond's supply loss came from landlords exiting through condo conversion and redevelopment, and those exits can be regulated.
Cities can restrict condo conversions, require just-cause eviction protections, and tie caps to inflation so landlords keep real returns.
Oregon's law does this: 7 percent plus inflation, new buildings exempt for 15 years.
Con calls that not real rent control, yet it still protects families from the sudden spikes that cause displacement.
Con's own St. Paul example shows a city correcting course within a year.
The same study found covered tenants were far more likely to stay put.
Cities should adopt stabilization with safeguards.
PRO's safeguards do not rescue rent control.
Restricting condo conversions and requiring just-cause eviction cannot force landlords to maintain aging units once returns fall below costs; deferred maintenance is standard under caps.
Oregon's 7 percent plus inflation is not a cap that prevents displacement; in high-inflation years it permits double-digit increases, and its 15-year new-building exemption simply delays the cliff.
St. Paul's reversal after one year shows the policy failed, not that it worked.
Diamond found the supply loss and higher rents for non-covered tenants.
Cities should reject rent control because it transfers housing security from future renters to current ones.
Charging drivers to enter busy city centres can reduce congestion while funding alternatives to driving.
London introduced its congestion charge in February 2003; Transport for London reported that traffic entering the charging zone fell by about 18% in the first year.
Stockholm’s 2006 congestion-charge trial reduced traffic across the cordon by about 20%, and the system became permanent in 2007.
These results show that a fee can change travel choices, not merely raise money.
Cities should pair charges with reliable public transport and sensible exemptions, so people have practical alternatives and those with legitimate needs are not unfairly burdened.
The evidence PRO cites shows that fees move traffic, not that they deliver lasting benefits or fairness.

London's own experience is instructive: Transport for London's later reports found congestion returned to roughly pre-charge levels by the early 2010s, even as vehicle numbers entering the zone stayed lower, because road space was reallocated to buses, cycle lanes and works.
Speed gains faded.
The deeper problem is fairness.
A flat fee is regressive: it costs a cleaner on a low wage the same as a banker, yet the wealthy can simply absorb it.
Cities also differ from London and Stockholm, which already had dense rail and metro networks.
Where alternatives are thin, a fee is a tax on necessity.
It also pushes shoppers toward out-of-town retail, hurting central small businesses.
Congestion returning as London reallocated road space does not show the charge failed: it shows that less road capacity was available, while fewer vehicles still entered the zone.
The charge manages demand, not a promise of permanently faster journeys.
Nor must fairness mean charging everyone identically.
Cities can provide exemptions or discounts for people with disabilities and targeted help where alternatives are poor.
London’s congestion-charge revenue is legally required to support transport improvements, which can widen alternatives over time.
Without a fee, drivers still pay through time lost in traffic, but that cost is hidden and shared by everyone.
A carefully designed charge makes scarce centre-road space less wasteful.
PRO concedes the key point: the charge no longer delivers faster journeys in London.
If the benefit is only "demand management" while congestion is back, residents are paying for a policy whose headline justification has lapsed.
Exemptions also cut against the design.
London's charge gives a 90% residents' discount inside the zone and exempts Blue Badge holders, and every carve-out erodes both revenue and traffic reduction, while adding administration.
Targeted help for low-income drivers is a promise, not the policy as usually implemented.
As for the claim that time lost is a hidden cost, a fee does not remove it; it adds a money cost on top for those who still must drive.
Better tools exist: bus priority, parking pricing and investment in transit, which do not tax access to the centre.
A charge need not guarantee permanently faster journeys to be worthwhile: it can prevent traffic from being worse than it otherwise would be and price scarce road space.
London’s charge is not simply an extra cost layered onto unchanged traffic; TfL reports that traffic entering the zone fell after introduction, and the fee funds transport improvements.
Bus priority and transit investment are valuable, but they do not by themselves manage the number of cars seeking limited centre-road space.
Design matters: cities can phase in charges only where practical alternatives exist, with targeted exemptions and support rather than abandoning the tool altogether.
The fair comparison is not free access, but who bears congestion’s costs.
PRO's final position is now conditional: charge only where good alternatives exist, with exemptions and support.
That concedes my core point, that a flat entry fee is the wrong tool for most cities, which lack London's or Stockholm's rail networks.
The "worse than it otherwise would be" claim is also unprovable, since no one can observe the counterfactual.
Meanwhile the costs are real.
London's scheme costs a large share of its revenue to operate; TfL's own figures have put operating costs at roughly half of gross revenue in early years.
Parking pricing, bus lanes and transit investment manage demand without taxing access to the centre.
Cities should use those first.
London's congestion charge, launched in February 2003 at £5, cut traffic entering the central zone by roughly 20 percent in its first year, according to Transport for London.
Stockholm's 2006 trial reduced cross-cordon traffic about 20 percent, and voters made it permanent in 2007.
Singapore pioneered the idea in 1975.
Charges work because they price the scarce road space, cutting congestion, emissions and journey times while raising revenue for buses and trains.
Drivers still choose to pay when a trip is worth it.
The alternative, free gridlock, costs everyone more.
London's own record undercuts PRO.
Transport for London's monitoring reports found that by around 2007 central congestion had drifted back toward pre-charge levels, even as the fee rose from £5 to £8, and it now stands at £15.
Traffic fell, but the jams returned, so drivers keep paying ever more for little lasting gain.
That is a flat tax that weighs most on tradespeople, carers and lower-income commuters without good transit, while the wealthy barely notice.
Voters have seen this: Edinburgh rejected a charge by about three to one in 2005, and Greater Manchester by roughly 79 percent in 2008.
Better transit, smarter signals and parking policy can ease traffic without tolling citizens out of their own city.
Stockholm's 2007 referendum is the answer: voters backed the charge once they saw 20% less traffic and cleaner air, so Edinburgh and Manchester rejected untested schemes, not the policy.
London's rebound came from reallocated road space and construction, not the charge; TfL still recorded fewer vehicles entering than before 2003.
Charges are not flat: London gives residents 90% off and reinvests revenue in buses.
A fee that shifts trips to transit and funds alternatives is fairer than free roads rationed by endless delay.
PRO's Stockholm example is weaker than it sounds.

The referendum was held in September 2006, and only about 53 percent of Stockholm city voters backed the charge, while most surrounding municipalities, whose commuters actually pay, voted no in their own consultations.
The national government made it permanent anyway.
That is a narrow urban majority taxing suburban outsiders.
PRO concedes London's congestion returned and blames construction and reallocated road space.
If street works and design choices can wipe out the charge's congestion benefit, then road management, not tolling, is the decisive lever.
The residents' discount proves my point on fairness: insiders get 90 percent off while the carer or plumber driving in from outside pays the full £15.

CON's Stockholm objection is political, not practical: the trial cut traffic about 20%, city voters saw it and backed permanence, and suburban no votes can be answered by earmarking revenue for park-and-ride and buses.
London's rebound shows charges must be paired with road management—not that free roads work.
On fairness, the £15 full fee is not inevitable: London already exempts disabled drivers, and cities can discount off-peak trades.
Someone must ration scarce central road space; pricing does it efficiently and funds alternatives.
Free gridlock is the regressive option.
PRO's final answer concedes my central point: London's charge only works when paired with road management, because street works and design choices erased its congestion gains.
If management is the decisive lever, cities should lead with it rather than taxing entry.
PRO's fairness fixes prove the problem too.
Every new exemption, for disabled drivers, residents or tradespeople, narrows the base, so the remaining payers, often suburban commuters without good transit, carry more of the cost.
Stockholm's surrounding municipalities voted no and the charge was imposed anyway.
Rationing road space by price means rationing by wealth.
Investing in transit, smarter signals and parking policy eases congestion without pricing ordinary people out of their own city centres.
